# Profiles, Preferences, History, and Ambient Context

Yantra keeps personal defaults and task records on the local machine. You can
inspect the effective profile, override individual preferences, control whether
the agent receives your configured location, list run history, and summarize
indexed task cost without giving raw prior-task text to a language model.

This personal profile is separate from the Chrome profiles used by saved
workflows.

## What It Does

### Resolves one effective personal profile

Yantra combines two storage layers into the view shown by `yantra profile`:

| Layer                          | Contents                                                                                           | Provenance shown by `yantra profile` |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `profile.yaml`                 | Human-editable defaults, locale values, context grants, personalization values, and agent defaults | `profile.yaml`                       |
| `index.db` `preferences` table | Values written with `yantra prefs set` and any machine-learned values                              | `index.db`                           |

For the same key, an explicit `prefs set` user row wins over
`profile.yaml`, which wins over a learned row. User-authored YAML values and
`prefs set` rows are approved by definition. A learned row starts unapproved
and must be approved before it can contribute to model-facing personalization.

There are two different read surfaces:

- `yantra profile` shows the merged effective view, including built-in values
  supplied when `profile.yaml` is absent or partial.
- `yantra prefs get` and `yantra prefs list` read only rows stored in
  `index.db`; they do not show values that exist only in `profile.yaml`.

The profile currently affects commands in these ways:

- Model-backed `ask` uses the approved personalization summary and the ambient
  context described below. Its unset `--detail`, `--length`, and
  `--search-provider` options resolve from `defaults.*`.
- Agentic `ask`, `research`, and `do` resolve their shared provider/model and
  runtime options from `agent.*`, and all three receive ambient context.
- `run` and `resume` use `agent.*` when selecting optional model-written replay
  synthesis. They do not receive the agentic ambient block.
- `research` presentation/search options and `do` task behavior do not consume
  `defaults.detail`, `defaults.length`, or `defaults.search_provider`.

Personal preferences do not grant tools or weaken command safety. The fixed
least-privilege command profiles still decide which web, browser, workflow, and
publication tools `ask`, `research`, and `do` may use.

See [Usage](../usage.md) for the shared agent option
flags, environment variables, duration syntax, and pinned defaults.

### Builds bounded, approved personalization

On a model-backed `ask`, Yantra can add a short reader-context paragraph made
from approved preferences. The current builder can include:

- `locale.units` as a unit preference;
- `locale.region` as a “Based in” statement;
- `personalization.favorite_retailers`; and
- `personalization.interests`.

It does not include operational `agent.*` settings. Setting
`personalization.enabled` to `false` suppresses the whole paragraph. Otherwise,
the paragraph is sanitized, limited to 400 characters at a sentence boundary,
and passed to the model only on the current `ask` model path. Agentic
`research`, `do`, and replay synthesis do not currently receive this paragraph.

The builder accepts effective preferences only. It has no input for a history
row, and a property test plus a build-time import-graph check enforce that raw
history intent text cannot enter an LLM payload through personalization.

### States ambient run facts without guessing location

Every agentic `ask`, `research`, and `do` run supplies an authoritative ambient
block containing:

- the current date, including weekday;
- the host IANA timezone and its DST-correct UTC offset;
- the host BCP 47 locale tag; and
- either the granted user location or the literal `not available`.

The date, timezone, and locale tag come from the host clock and environment.
They are always supplied and are not controlled by `locale.region` or a context
grant.

User location is different. `context.location` gates a value composed, in
order, from approved `locale.city` and `locale.region` values. The composed
value is sanitized and capped at 120 characters. When the grant is off, the
values are absent, or the winning values are unapproved, the model sees only:

```text
- user location: not available
```

Denied and unconfigured location are intentionally indistinguishable in the
model prompt. The closing ambient rule tells the model never to infer a missing
fact from timezone or locale.

For clearly self-referential goals such as “hotels near me” or “in my area,” a
deterministic preflight stops before a provider session or browser is opened if
location is unavailable. The command exits with a human handoff and tells you
either to set `locale.city` or re-enable `context.location`. A goal with its own
anchor, such as “nearest station to Times Square,” is not blocked.

The location grant applies to the ambient location slot. The separate `ask`
personalization paragraph can still include an approved `locale.region` as a
“Based in” preference. To keep the region out of every model-facing context,
also set `locale.region` to `null` or disable personalization.

### Keeps local run history and usage summaries

The `history` table in the local SQLite index stores one row per indexed task:
run ID, task type (`ask`, `research`, `run`, or `do`), intent text, document ID,
terminal status, start/end time, duration, provider, and cost when available.
Intent text remains local history and is not an input to personalization.

`yantra list runs` merges indexed rows with the file-based run store, de-duplicates
by run ID, sorts newest first, and then applies its filters. This lets listing
continue from run files even when the index cannot be read. `yantra show`
inspects the canonical run directory rather than the history row.

`yantra usage` reads the history index only. It groups task count and known cost
by stored calendar day and provider, then prints totals. Missing or unmetered
cost contributes zero; this command is a task/cost rollup, not the per-turn
token ledger in each run's `usage.json`.

The same database also persists per-host rate-limit buckets, so an exhausted
host does not receive a fresh burst merely because Yantra restarts. If the
index cannot be opened, the ethics gate falls back to process-local buckets.

## How to Use It

### Initialize the profile

```bash
yantra init
yantra init --yes
yantra init --json
yantra init --reset
```

`init` writes `config.yaml` and, when needed, `profile.yaml`. On an interactive
TTY without `--json` or `--yes`, it asks whether the agent may receive your
location. Accepting prompts for an optional city or area; declining stores the
grant as `false` and does not ask for a city.

Prompting occurs only when the profile will be written: on first initialization
or `--reset`. A non-TTY, `--json`, `--yes`, cancellation, or an ordinary rerun
uses the defaults without prompting. The default is a granted location with no
city configured, which still renders as `not available`.

`--reset` backs up `config.yaml` and rewrites the profile from defaults and new
answers. Without `--reset`, an existing config makes `init` return
`already-initialized` without changing the profile.

### Inspect preferences

```bash
yantra profile
yantra profile --json

yantra prefs list
yantra prefs get defaults.detail
yantra prefs list --json
```

`profile` is the answer to “what value will Yantra use, and from which layer?”
It prints the resolved value and provenance for every key. `prefs list` and
`prefs get` answer “what is stored in the SQLite preference layer?”

The non-JSON profile output also prints the resolved `profile.yaml` path. It is
yours to edit directly.

### Set or approve a preference

```bash
yantra prefs set defaults.detail full
yantra prefs set defaults.length long
yantra prefs set defaults.search_provider brave
yantra prefs set locale.units imperial
yantra prefs set locale.city "Naperville, IL"
yantra prefs set locale.region US
yantra prefs set personalization.interests "browser automation,local AI"
yantra prefs set personalization.favorite_retailers "Target,Best Buy"
yantra prefs set personalization.enabled false
yantra prefs set context.location false

yantra prefs approve personalization.interests
```

Boolean values must be `true` or `false`. List values are comma-separated.
`locale.city`, `locale.region`, `agent.provider`, `agent.model`, and
`agent.thinking` accept the literal `null` where their schemas allow it.
Unknown keys and invalid enum, duration, or numeric values fail validation.

`prefs approve` is intended for a stored learned row. It prints `not-found` in
JSON and exits with a validation error when the key has no SQLite row. The
current CLI does not itself create learned rows; that source is available to
integrations and future learning code.

### Forget an override

```bash
yantra prefs --forget defaults.detail
```

This permanently deletes the matching row from the SQLite `preferences` table.
It does **not** edit `profile.yaml`. If the same key is present there, the
effective value immediately falls back to the YAML value. To remove or change a
YAML value, edit `profile.yaml` directly. Removing a YAML key usually restores
that key's built-in schema default.

For example, to clear a SQLite location override while retaining YAML fallback:

```bash
yantra prefs --forget locale.city
```

To override a YAML city with no city in the effective profile:

```bash
yantra prefs set locale.city null
```

For run-scoped sensitive input and durable website/model credentials, use the
separate controls documented in [Safety and Privacy](safety-and-privacy.md)
and [Agentic Tasks](agentic-tasks.md#configuration-and-permissions). Those
values are not profile preferences.

### List, inspect, and summarize runs

```bash
yantra list
yantra list runs --limit 5
yantra list runs --workflow quarterly-report --status failed
yantra list runs --json

yantra show 20260815T120000Z-quarterly-report-a1b2c3d4
yantra show 20260815T120000Z-quarterly-report-a1b2c3d4 --run --events 50
yantra show 20260815T120000Z-quarterly-report-a1b2c3d4 --json

yantra usage
yantra usage --type ask --since 7d
yantra usage --type research --since 24h
yantra usage --since 2026-08-01 --json
```

`list` defaults to `runs` and a limit of 20. Limits above 500 are capped at
500; an invalid or non-positive value falls back to 20. `--workflow` and
`--status` are exact string filters applied after file/index merging.

`show` auto-detects a compact timestamp-prefixed target as a run ID. Use
`--run` or `--workflow` to override detection. A run display contains the full
manifest plus the requested tail of parseable `events.jsonl` records; the
default is 20 and the maximum is 1,000. Use the run ID with `yantra audit` or
`yantra report` for the wider durable trail described in
[Diagnostics and Audit](diagnostics-and-audit.md).

`usage --since` accepts `YYYY-MM-DD`, an integer number of days such as `7d`, or
an integer number of hours such as `24h`. `--type` accepts only `ask`,
`research`, `run`, or `do`.

Run `yantra doctor` to check that the index is writable. If SQLite corruption
is detected, Yantra moves the old file to an `index.db.corrupt.<timestamp>`
side file, creates a new schema, and rebuilds the `history` table from terminal
run manifests.

## Inputs and Outputs

### Preference keys

| Keys                                                                | Accepted values and current use                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `defaults.search_provider`                                          | `auto`, `google`, `duckduckgo`, `brave`, or `tavily`; unset `ask --search-provider` |
| `defaults.detail`                                                   | `overview`, `standard`, or `full`; unset `ask --detail`                             |
| `defaults.length`                                                   | `short`, `medium`, or `long`; unset `ask --length`                                  |
| `locale.city`                                                       | Non-blank string or `null`; granted ambient location                                |
| `locale.region`                                                     | String or `null`; granted ambient location and `ask` personalization                |
| `locale.units`                                                      | `metric` or `imperial`; `ask` personalization                                       |
| `context.location`                                                  | Boolean; permits the ambient location value                                         |
| `personalization.enabled`                                           | Boolean; master switch for the `ask` personalization paragraph                      |
| `personalization.interests`                                         | String list; `ask` personalization                                                  |
| `personalization.favorite_retailers`                                | String list; `ask` personalization                                                  |
| `agent.provider`, `agent.model`, `agent.thinking`                   | Non-blank string or `null`; model/session selection only                            |
| `agent.max_duration`, `agent.tool_timeout`, `agent.confirm_timeout` | Positive duration: integer with optional `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h` suffix              |
| `agent.max_tokens`                                                  | Positive integer                                                                    |
| `agent.tool_retries`                                                | Non-negative integer                                                                |

### Human and JSON output

Every JSON form carries `schemaVersion` plus a command-specific `kind`.

| Command                      | Human output                                                | JSON payload highlights                                                                 |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `profile`                    | Profile path and sorted effective key/value/provenance rows | `kind: "profile"`, `profilePath`, `preferences[]` with source, approval, and provenance |
| `prefs list`                 | Sorted SQLite rows with user/learned approval state         | `kind: "prefs"`, `rows[]`                                                               |
| `prefs get`                  | Stored value or “is not set”                                | `kind: "prefs"`, `key`, nullable `record`                                               |
| `prefs set/approve/--forget` | Short status line                                           | `kind: "prefs"`, `status`, `key`, and the validated value for `set`                     |
| `list`                       | Run/workflow rows; `No items.` when empty                   | `kind: "list"`, `items[]`                                                               |
| `show`                       | Parsed workflow or run manifest and event tail              | `kind: "show"`, discriminated `item`                                                    |
| `usage`                      | Day/provider task and cost table plus totals                | `kind: "usage"`, `rows[]`, `totals`                                                     |

History rows use `succeeded`, `failed`, `handoff`, and `aborted`. File-backed
workflow runs use manifest statuses such as `running`, `completed`, `failed`,
`aborted`, and `paused`. The list renderer preserves the source status rather
than normalizing both vocabularies.

### Errors and fallback behavior

- `prefs set` exits 1 for an unknown key or invalid value. Missing positional
  arguments and unknown actions also exit 1.
- `prefs approve` exits 1 when no stored row exists. `prefs --forget` is
  idempotent and exits 0 with `not-found`/“was not set” when there was no row.
- A preference-index open failure makes mutating/read-row `prefs` commands exit
  3 with a `yantra doctor` remedy. Effective profile reads continue with the
  YAML/default layer.
- `list` exits 1 for an unknown target. If the history index cannot be opened,
  it prints a note and lists file-backed runs only.
- `show` exits 1 when the requested workflow or run directory cannot be found.
  Unparseable event lines are skipped instead of failing the whole display.
- `usage` exits 1 for an invalid type or `--since` value. If the index cannot be
  opened, it emits an empty rollup with a rebuild note and exits 0.
- A location-dependent agentic goal with no location produces a handoff (exit
  4), a run report, and no provider-token or browser work.

## Configuration and Permissions

### Local paths

| State               | Windows                               | Linux/macOS default                   |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Personal profile    | `%APPDATA%\yantra\profile.yaml`       | `~/.config/yantra/profile.yaml`       |
| Shared SQLite index | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\yantra\index.db`      | `~/.local/share/yantra/index.db`      |
| Canonical runs      | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\yantra\runs\<run-id>` | `~/.local/share/yantra/runs/<run-id>` |

On Linux and macOS, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `XDG_DATA_HOME` override the default
roots. Yantra writes profile and index files with owner-only `0600` permissions
and their directories with `0700` where POSIX permissions apply. Windows uses
the current account's inherited ACLs.

The SQLite connection uses WAL mode and foreign-key enforcement. The shared
database currently contains `history`, `preferences`, `rate_limits`,
`schedules`, `domain_ranks`, and `meta` tables. Only `history` is reconstructable
from run directories. Preference overrides, schedules, rate-limit state, and
domain ranks are not restored by a history rebuild; back up `index.db` if those
local records matter. Scheduling has additional storage semantics documented in
[Scheduling and the Local Daemon](scheduling.md#configuration-and-permissions).

### Resolution precedence

For `ask` detail, length, and search-provider defaults:

```text
explicit command flag
  > index.db user row (`prefs set`)
  > profile.yaml
  > learned index.db row
  > command built-in
```

For shared `agent.*` options:

```text
explicit command flag
  > environment variable
  > effective preference (using the three profile layers above)
  > pinned agent default
```

`--no-llm` or `LLM_PROVIDER=none` is resolved before unused model settings are
validated.

### Privacy and retention boundaries

- Stored profile, preference, and history data is local filesystem data. When a
  model-backed command runs, the approved bounded personalization and the
  documented ambient facts are sent as part of that provider session.
- Raw history intent text is not used as personalization. The model-facing
  builders accept preference values only, sanitize their output, and are
  protected by property and import-graph tests.
- Operational `agent.*` preferences configure enforcement and session startup;
  they are excluded from the personalization paragraph.
- Run artifacts remain the durable record. `config.yaml` is initialized with
  `retention.runsDays: 30`, but the current CLI does not enforce that value and
  registers no history-clean/prune command. Run directories remain until you
  remove them outside Yantra.
- There is no CLI command to delete an individual history row or run directory.
  Deleting a run directory does not immediately remove an existing index row.
- A corrupt database is moved aside rather than erased. That recovery copy may
  still contain personal preferences and history and should be protected like
  the active database.

## Limitations

- The incremental history index is not currently exhaustive. Completed
  deterministic and agentic `ask`, published agentic `research`, completed
  direct `run`, and scheduled fires have recording paths. Ordinary published
  `do` is currently indexed on the templated-report path only, deterministic
  `research` does not record at completion, and failed/handoff agentic commands
  are not all upserted. `list runs` can still discover terminal run directories,
  but `usage` can omit those tasks until a corruption recovery rebuilds history.
- Removing a merely healthy `index.db` creates a fresh empty database on the
  next open; the automatic run-tree rebuild hook currently runs on detected
  corruption, not on an absent file. `list` still merges canonical run files,
  while `usage` begins empty.
- `--status` is an exact filter over mixed history and file-manifest status
  vocabularies. For example, an indexed successful task is `succeeded`, while a
  file-backed completed workflow is `completed`.
- `prefs --forget` deletes only the SQLite row. There is no CLI writer for
  removing a key from `profile.yaml`, and no command that deletes both layers.
- The current CLI has no producer for learned preference rows. Approval and
  merge behavior are implemented for integrations, but normal `prefs set`
  always writes an approved user row.
- A present but invalid `profile.yaml` is rejected by the core schema, but the
  current effective-profile CLI helper warns only through its logger and falls
  back to built-in defaults. Run `yantra profile --debug` when diagnosing a
  hand-edited file.
- Location preflight deliberately matches only conservative self-referential
  phrases. Other location-dependent goals rely on the explicit
  `not available` marker and the model instruction not to derive missing facts.
- `profile`, `prefs`, `list`, `show`, and `usage` are local CLI surfaces. There
  is no remote profile sync, history UI, automatic retention enforcement, or
  supported bulk export/import command.
